title: the Gayatri in context
hook: a line on a coffee mug once had a whole speech around it. so does the Gayatri

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta, and its ending: with the offering, they offered to the offering, a giving that feeds the next giving. What did you pass on that someone once gave you? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.
screen: `A GIVING THAT FEEDS THE NEXT GIVING.`

segments.voice: A line printed on a coffee mug. A sentence someone tattooed on a wrist. A quote pinned above a desk. Each one came out of something bigger: a speech, a letter, a chapter, with a speaker and a room and a moment around it. The line still works on its own. But put it back where it came from, and it says a little more. The Gayatri is often heard on its own: at dawn, at a thread ceremony, on a phone before an exam. For the next six days, this path puts it back on its string. Today: the hymn it lives in.
screen: `A LINE ON A MUG.` → `IT CAME FROM SOMETHING BIGGER.` → `PUT IT BACK ON ITS STRING.`

segments.voice: The verse sits in the Rig Veda, book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. In Sanskrit it begins tat savitur varenyam, and it ends dhiyo yo nah prachodayat: may he stir our thoughts. Now open the hymn around it. Hymn sixty-two is not a hymn to one god. It moves, in small groups of verses, from one to another. It opens by calling on Indra and Varuna together. Then it turns to Brihaspati, the lord of prayer. Then to Pushan, the god of roads and safe journeys. Then, partway through, it turns to Savitr, the sun who sets things moving. That turn is the Gayatri. It's the first verse to Savitr, and the verses after it keep speaking to him for a little while, asking for his gifts. Then the hymn moves on again: to Soma, and to Mitra and Varuna. So inside its own hymn, the Gayatri is one voice in a chorus. A neighbor among neighbors. It doesn't stand at the beginning or the end. It stands in the middle, at the moment the hymn faces the sun. Later Hindu practice lifted this one verse out and gave it a life of its own: at the twilight prayers, at the sacred thread ceremony, on strings of beads. That lifting-out is part of its story too. Tradition chose this verse, from this hymn, and kept it close. Knowing the neighbors doesn't make it smaller. It shows where it was standing when someone first said, this one.
screen: `BOOK THREE, HYMN SIXTY-TWO.` · `A HYMN THAT TURNS FROM GOD TO GOD.` · `THE FIRST VERSE TO SAVITR.` · `LIFTED OUT, KEPT ON ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a verse with its neighbors. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the last line's meaning: may our thoughts be stirred. If your tradition welcomes you to say the Sanskrit, you can say dhiyo yo nah prachodayat, softly. If not, the English meaning is enough. Then widen. Notice what's around you: the floor, the walls, the sounds beyond them, the people in the next room or the next street. Let the line sit in the middle of all of it, the way the verse sits in the middle of its hymn. The bell holds the time.
The Gayatri in context. Rig Veda three, sixty-two, ten: one verse in a hymn that turns from god to god, the first of its verses to Savitr. Today's word.
Your line: the Gayatri in context. Today, when a single line catches you, a quote, a lyric, a sentence in an email, go find what came before and after it. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Hindus who keep the practice recite the Gayatri on its own, at dawn and dusk or with a mala; in Vedic recitation it is also learned as part of Rig Veda 3.62, the hymn it comes from.

original.note: Sanskrit: Savitr, the god the Gayatri speaks to; in the verse his name appears as savitur, 'of Savitr'.

what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 3.62 is built from small groups of verses to different gods, and later practice singled out verse ten.
